title: When Lightning Strikes … Sometimes It Results in an Incredible Chair
summary: Italian architect and designer Paolo Pallucco was inspired to create a visionary series of chairs.
body_markdown:
[Paolo Pallucco Sedia No. 6, 1990](https://www.1stdibs.com/furniture/seating/chairs/sedia-da-temporale-fulminata-alle-spalle-paolo-pallucco/id-f_48672192/) , offered by by[Ketabi Bourdet Design](https://www.1stdibs.com/dealers/ketabi-bourdet-design/)


A lightning strike is a potent metaphor for sudden clarity, a flash of brilliance or a life-changing event.[Paolo Pallucco](https://www.1stdibs.com/creators/paolo-pallucco/furniture/) ’s lightning moment was all these things. Upon hearing a savvy gallerist recite Rainer Maria Rilke’s poem “Alcestis,” the Italian architect and designer had an epiphany that inspired his visionary series “100 Sedie in una Notte” (“100 Chairs in One Night”).


The aptly named project used the form of the chair to explore the connections between poetry, philosophy, design and sculpture. Of the 100 chair designs he conceived, the Sedia No. 6, an example of which is currently being offered on 1stDibs by[Ketabi Bourdet Design](https://www.1stdibs.com/dealers/ketabi-bourdet-design/) , is perhaps the most electric.


Before launching the series, in 1990, Pallucco had made a name for himself with the eponymous lighting and furniture company he founded a decade earlier. He was a leader in iconic-design reeditions and created notable Radical Design and postmodern works that helped define Italian design in the 1980s. By the end of that decade, he had reached a “what next?” juncture, and Rilke’s poem was the impetus he needed to conceive his next monumental project.


In “Alcestis,” Rilke retells the mythological story of a desperate bridegroom who pleads with the god of death for one more night after learning his death is imminent. For Pallucco, the plea raised a profound question about his work as a designer. As he put it in his essay introducing the project, “How would I have used those hours of extension, “How would I have used those hours of extension, and what project would have satisfied that sliver of professional ambition and at the same time fulfilled the vexation of the impertinent god?”


Pallucco’s “100 Sedie in una Notte” (“100 Chairs in One Night”)


The answer lay in the humble chair. The chair, Pallucco later explained, is so common and practical that it is nearly impossible for a designer to conceive of an example that is truly new or surprising. Inspired by the bridegroom’s plea, he set out to design “100 Sedie in una Notte” as a magnum opus of sorts.


Beginning with Sedia No. 1, a simple black structure, the series evolved into an exploration of the fundamental concepts shaping the human experience. With[No. 6, Sedia da Temporale Fulminata alle Spalle](https://www.1stdibs.com/furniture/seating/chairs/sedia-da-temporale-fulminata-alle-spalle-paolo-pallucco/id-f_48672192/) (“Storm Chair Struck by Lightning from Behind”), Pallucco found a language to express the multilayered essence of his project. Its simple black structure is strikingly graphic and sculptural and rich in symbolic possibilities, evoking a host of existential questions: Is it the physical manifestation of the brilliant ideas that might come to a sitter or the residue of a sinister, ill-fated moment in an electric chair? Perhaps this is not a functional chair at all but a sculpture — or a poem made visible, emerging from the ether.


Another chair in Pallucco’s series,[No. 24, Sedia Sarcastica sulla Propria Sorte (Sarcastic Chair about One’s Own Destiny)](https://www.1stdibs.com/furniture/seating/chairs/paolo-pallucco-sedia-no24-chair-1990-italy/id-f_35951042/) , 1990, is also offered by[Ketabi Bourdet Design](https://www.1stdibs.com/dealers/ketabi-bourdet-design/) .


“100 Sedie in una Notte” is a virtuosic accomplishment: a dazzling array of inventive forms, made more compelling by the questions they raise about the meaning of life, the concept of time and the boundaries of the physical world. Is it possible to start anew, leaving the present behind, as suggested by No. 57, Sedia Che si Butta il Presente alle Spalle (Chair That Leaves the Present Behind)? Or is life an eternal return, playing out on an infinite loop, as posited by No. 58, Sedia d’Appoggio dell’Eterno Ritorno (Support Chair of the Eternal Return)? Are there moments that can forever change the form of things, as implied by the morphing structure of No. 69, Sedia Sorpresa durante l’Incontro con una Forma Affascinante (Chair that Surprises during the Encounter with a Fascinating Shape)? Or are we taking things far too seriously, as implied by[No. 24, Sedia Sarcastica sulla Propria Sorte (Sarcastic Chair about One’s Own Destiny)](https://www.1stdibs.com/furniture/seating/chairs/paolo-pallucco-sedia-no24-chair-1990-italy/id-f_35951042/) ?


Each chair in the series was produced in an edition of four by the Galleria d’Arte Contemporanea Emilio Mazzoli, in Modena, Italy. Rare examples come to market from time to time, transformed by the context from verses in Pallucco’s epic 100-line “poem” to standalone sculptural concepts. Ketabi Bourdet’s[Sedia No. 6](https://www.1stdibs.com/furniture/seating/chairs/sedia-da-temporale-fulminata-alle-spalle-paolo-pallucco/id-f_48672192/) stands as a reminder of the flash of genius that can strike at any time, altering the course of one’s life and work, as it did for Pallucco.
